summary:
Bhutan decriminalised consensual same-sex intimacy in 2021. The lower house of Parliament voted 43-1 in June 2019 to repeal Penal Code Sections 213 and 214, the 'unnatural sex' provisions carrying one month to one year of imprisonment, which had gone unenforced for at least 15 years. The upper house reinserted the ban, and a December 2020 joint sitting resolved that homosexuality between adults shall not be considered unnatural sex. The Penal Code Amendment Act entered into force on 17 February 2021, and no reversal has followed.

The repeal created no protective framework. Bhutan has no stand-alone anti-discrimination law and no explicit protections on the grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, and sex characteristics. Discrimination and stigma persist, with health-care access singled out as a domain where trans and LGBTIQ people are turned away or poorly served.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable: administrative gender-marker changes are suspended for lack of standardised guidelines. Where markers can be changed at all, the process requires a medical note plus a supporting letter from a civil society organisation. A trans person's identity card therefore continues to display the sex assigned at birth, with direct consequences for how violence against them is treated.

Violence risk is elevated and reporting channels are effectively closed. Trans people are more than four times as likely to experience assault. A 49-year-old trans woman interviewed in November 2024 described police dismissing her cases because her identity card reads male, on the reasoning that 'both parties are men'; families pressure victims to accept the assault as fate, and assistance routed through the LGBTQIA+ committee is slow. The result is practical impunity for anti-trans violence despite formal decriminalisation.

Entry and visa rules carry no trans-specific screening provisions in the sources reviewed. Bhutan provides no legal recognition of same-sex relationships, and partners of trans and other LGBTQ people cannot be recognised in any legal proceeding. A marriage bill using gender-neutral pronouns was discussed during the 2018 summer parliamentary session but deferred because of the 2018 parliamentary election.

Some protective instruments exist at sectoral level. The Bhutan Medical and Health Council's Code of Professional Fidelity, issued in 2021, protects sexual orientation. The 2020 Standard Operating Procedure for Gender Based Violence Prevention and Response requires healthcare providers to deliver age-appropriate, culturally sensitive, and sexual orientation and gender identity sensitive care, and requires case managers to provide tailored care for people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities. The National Strategic Framework on Comprehensive Sexuality Education (2021) covers LGBTI issues.

Official engagement has increased without producing legislation. The 2024 Free & Equal campaign trained the Royal Court of Justice, the Attorney General's Office and the Cabinet Secretariat, and secured the first direct dialogue between Bhutan's LGBTIQ+ community and parliamentarians. Two consultation workshops convened community members with UN and National Commission for Women and Children representatives.
tangentialFactors:
Public trans visibility remains exceptional. A Bhutan Broadcasting Service feature profiles Dechen, one of only two trans women living publicly, who at 16 fought to wear the female school uniform kira, described as a first in Bhutanese society. The LGBT Bhutan Facebook page, launched around 2014, produced the country's first public affirmation of a gay population.

Social invisibility is the more common condition. Reporting from 2015 found LGBT Bhutanese describing very little persecution or violence but near-total social invisibility, with one account stating that growing up gay in Bhutan was a very alienating experience. There is no shared language for gay or trans identities, and lesbianism is under-recognised.

Education outcomes are weak despite the sexuality-education framework: Rainbow Bhutan's director states that most LGBTQ youths drop out of school, and of the 316 people registered as LGBTQ in 2019, 10 were below age 19.
localsOnly:
LGBTIQ organisations may register, though activists describe the process as lengthy and burdensome.

Changing the gender marker on legal identification documents requires a medical note plus a supporting letter from a civil society organisation, and administrative changes are currently suspended for lack of standardised guidelines.

The 2024 Free & Equal campaign trained the Royal Court of Justice, Attorney General's Office and Cabinet Secretariat, and produced the first direct dialogue between the LGBTIQ+ community and parliamentarians. Two consultation workshops brought community members together with UN and National Commission for Women and Children representatives.

Rainbow Bhutan's director Tashi Tsheten called the 2019 lower-house vote 'our first journey towards equality'. Karma Dupchen, one of the most public LGBT figures, founded the LGBT Bhutan Facebook page in 2013.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not address entry, visa, or border-screening rules as they apply to trans travellers, and no finding on that question should be read from this record.

Whether the suspended gender-marker process has been replaced by new standardised guidelines since the Outright International overview was updated on 12 March 2026 is unresolved in the inventory.

The status of the deferred gender-neutral marriage bill under the current Parliament is unresolved; the inventory records only the 2018 deferral and the community expectation that the conversation would be revived.

Enforcement of the 2020 gender-based-violence standard operating procedure and the 2021 medical council code in reported cases is not documented in the sources reviewed.
